code.title: Count reallocations of push_back

followUps:
With growth by 2x, the old block is freed, but a new block of twice the size must coexist with it during copying; with 1.5x the freed blocks can eventually add up to enough room to be reused.

Example: sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9... With factor 2 each new block is bigger than the sum of all earlier blocks (1+2+4 < 8), so the allocator can never reuse that freed memory. With 1.5x the sum of old blocks eventually exceeds the next request, so freed memory can be recycled and fragmentation drops. The price is more reallocations: about log1.5 n instead of log2 n, still amortized O(1).

If copying or moving an element throws during growth, push_back gives the strong guarantee: the vector is left exactly as it was before the call.

To do that the vector builds the new block first and only then frees the old one. Moving is cheaper than copying, but a move that throws halfway would leave the old block damaged. So the library uses std::move_if_noexcept: it moves elements only if the move constructor is noexcept (or the type cannot be copied), and otherwise copies. Mark your move constructors noexcept or vector will silently copy on every growth.

Peak memory is the old block plus the new block at the same time, so roughly 3x the old capacity for a growth factor of 2 (old 1x + new 2x).

Example: a vector of 1,000,000 ints (4 MB) that is full needs a new 8 MB block while the old 4 MB block still holds the data, so for a moment 12 MB are in use. With factor 1.5 the peak is 2.5x. If memory is tight, call reserve with the final size, or use shrink_to_fit afterwards to give back unused capacity.

code.title: Which containers keep addresses stable

followUps:
Use sanitizers and debug standard-library modes: they catch most invalid-iterator uses while you run your tests.

Compile with -fsanitize=address,undefined (AddressSanitizer reports use-after-free when a vector reallocates and you read the old block). With GCC add -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG, which makes every iterator remember its container and aborts with a clear message when an invalidated one is used; MSVC debug builds do the same. Static analysers such as clang-tidy and linters also flag patterns like erasing inside a range-for loop. These checks slow the program, so use them in tests, not production.

Node-based containers (list, map, set) and, for references, deque on end insertions and unordered_map keep element addresses stable, and the price is extra memory and slower, scattered access.

Each element lives in its own heap node, so inserting elsewhere never moves it. The cost is a pointer or two per element (16 to 40 bytes), one allocation per insert, and poor cache behaviour. If you only need stability for a while, a vector<unique_ptr<T>> or a vector of indices also works: indices stay valid after reallocation even though addresses do not.

code.title: list splice and stable iterators

followUps:
A pool or pmr allocator makes list nodes cheap to allocate and keeps them close together, so the list loses less of its disadvantage, but a vector is usually still faster to scan.

The main costs of a list are one malloc per node and nodes scattered in memory. With std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource nodes come from one contiguous buffer: allocation becomes a pointer bump and traversal touches nearby cache lines. It narrows the gap, yet the list still stores two pointers per element, so a 4-byte int costs about 24 bytes. Measure both.

An intrusive list stores the next and prev pointers inside the object itself instead of in a separate node, so linking needs no allocation at all.

Kernels use it because an object (such as a task or a network buffer) can sit on several lists at once with no malloc, an object can unlink itself in O(1) knowing only its own address, and allocation failure cannot happen while linking. Example: a task struct holds list_head run_queue; list_head wait_queue;. In C++ see boost::intrusive::list. The drawback is that the element's lifetime must outlive its membership in the list.

code.title: Deque block and slot index math

followUps:
deque has no reserve() or data() because its storage is not one contiguous block, so there is no single capacity to reserve and no single pointer to hand out.

Elements are split into many fixed blocks, so &d[0] + 1 is not guaranteed to be &d[1] across a block boundary. Code expecting a contiguous array (C APIs, memcpy) cannot use a deque. The block map grows automatically and blocks are allocated one by one, which is why deque never copies elements on push_back, whereas a vector would.

A ring buffer is better when the maximum size is known and you want one contiguous allocation with no per-block allocation and predictable latency.

A ring buffer over a fixed array uses head and size; element i sits at (head + i) % cap. Push and pop at either end are O(1) with no allocation, which suits queues in real-time code, producers and consumers, and sliding windows. A deque is better when the size is unbounded or you need stable references while it grows. Example: a window of the last 5 sensor readings is a ring of 5 ints (20 bytes).

code.title: map order, bounds and stable iterators

followUps:
Every node is either red or black, and these rules together keep the tree balanced.

  1. The root is black.
  2. Every leaf (null pointer) counts as black.
  3. A red node never has a red child.
  4. Every path from a node down to its leaves has the same number of black nodes.

Rules 3 and 4 mean the longest path (alternating red and black) is at most twice the shortest (all black), so height is at most 2 log2(n+1). With n = 1,000,000 that is at most about 40 levels.

A flat_map keeps sorted keys in one array and a B-tree map keeps many keys per node, so both read memory in large contiguous chunks and are much more cache friendly than a binary tree.

std::map visits about log2 n scattered nodes (20 cache misses for a million keys). A B-tree node holds, say, 16 to 64 keys, so the same lookup touches 3 or 4 nodes. flat_map has the fastest lookup and iteration but O(n) insert and erase, so it suits read-mostly data. A B-tree map such as absl::btree_map keeps O(log n) updates and ordered iteration but gives up the iterator and address stability std::map has.

code.title: Buckets, load factor and rehash

followUps:
The worst case is O(n) when many keys land in the same bucket, because then a lookup walks one long chain; defend with a good hash and, for untrusted input, a randomized seed.

With 1000 keys all in one bucket every find costs up to 1000 comparisons. Causes: a weak hash (for example identity on keys that are multiples of the bucket count), or an attacker choosing keys to collide. Defences: a well-mixing hash such as splitmix64, a seed chosen at startup, or fall back to std::map, which guarantees O(log n). Keeping the load factor low also shortens chains.

Open-addressing tables store entries directly in one array, so a lookup usually touches one or two adjacent cache lines instead of chasing pointers.

std::unordered_map must keep references stable (the standard requires it), which forces one heap node per element and separate chaining. Open addressing probes neighbouring slots in the same array, often with SIMD-assisted metadata checks, so there is no per-node allocation and far less memory overhead. The costs: iterators and references are invalidated on rehash, and large values are best stored as pointers. Typical speed-ups are 2 to 5 times.

code.title: pair and struct keys with custom hash

followUps:
The hash must be consistent with equality because the table first uses the hash to pick a bucket and only then uses == to compare, so two keys that compare equal but hash differently would live in different buckets and never be found.

Rule: if a == b then hash(a) == hash(b). Example: if a case-insensitive equality treats "Hi" and "hi" as equal but the hash uses the raw characters, inserting "Hi" and looking up "hi" goes to a different bucket and finds nothing. The reverse is allowed: different keys may share a hash (a collision), they are then told apart by ==.

Heterogeneous (transparent) lookup lets you search a container with a type different from its key type, so you can look up a string_view in a map of std::string without creating a temporary string.

For ordered containers use a transparent comparator: map<string, int, less<>> then m.find(string_view("abc")) works since C++14. For unordered containers it arrives in C++20: provide a hasher and an equality with using is_transparent = void;. It avoids one allocation and a copy per lookup, which matters in hot paths.

code.title: Min-heap, max-heap and custom comparator

followUps:
pop() returns void because returning the element by value could lose it: if the copy or move constructor threw after the element was already removed, the value would be gone and could not be recovered.

So the API splits it into two steps: read with top() (a const reference, never throws), then call pop(). This is the strong exception guarantee design. Example: int x = pq.top(); pq.pop();. For move-only types, use T x = std::move(const_cast<T&>(pq.top())); pq.pop(); or keep elements in your own heap built on std::pop_heap.

priority_queue has no decrease-key, so you push a new entry with the smaller distance and ignore stale entries when they come out (lazy deletion).

pq.push({d[v], v});          // min-heap by distance
while (!pq.empty()) {
  auto [dist, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
  if (dist > d[u]) continue;   // stale entry, skip
  // relax edges, push improved neighbours
}

The heap can hold up to E entries, so the total is O(E log E) = O(E log V), the same order as with decrease-key.

code.title: LRU cache with list and unordered_map

followUps:
Turn the LRU into an LFU by adding a use count per key and keeping the keys grouped in lists by that count.

Use unordered_map<int, node> from key to {value, count, iterator}, and unordered_map<int, list<int>> from count to keys, plus minCount. On access, move the key from the list of count c to the list of c+1 (splice, O(1)); if the list for minCount became empty, increment minCount. On eviction remove the front of the list for minCount (least frequent, oldest among ties). All operations stay O(1).

Shard it by hashing the key into N independent LRU caches, each with its own mutex, so threads working on different shards never block each other.

Example: with 16 shards, shard = hash(key) % 16 and each shard holds capacity/16 entries. Lock contention drops roughly 16 times if keys are spread evenly. The trade-off is that eviction is approximate (the globally oldest key may survive if its shard is not full) and a hot key still serializes on its shard. Other options: a reader-writer approach that records accesses in a buffer and applies them in batches.

A vector cannot move an entry to the front in O(1): moving an element from the middle shifts everything in between, and erasing the oldest item from the front costs O(n) too.

With 100,000 entries each get would shift up to 100,000 elements. A vector also makes stored indices stale after every shift, so the hash map would have to be updated for every moved element. The list's splice relinks a node with a few pointer writes and keeps every other iterator valid, so both operations are O(1).

code.title: insert vs emplace vs try_emplace vs operator[]

followUps:
Only try_emplace, emplace and insert work for a non-default-constructible value type; operator[] does not compile, and insert_or_assign needs the value to be assignable.

Example: struct W { W(int); };. m[1] fails because it needs W(). m.try_emplace(1, 5) and m.emplace(1, 5) are fine. m.insert_or_assign(1, 5) is fine too when W has an assignment operator; if it has no assignment (for example a const member), it fails. To read without inserting, use find or at.

Since C++17, extract() detaches a node from the map without copying or reallocating, lets you edit the key, and insert() puts it back.

auto nh = m.extract(5);   // O(log n), no allocation
if (!nh.empty()) {
  nh.key() = 50;          // the key is writable here
  m.insert(std::move(nh));
}

Without it you would erase and insert, which destroys and rebuilds the element. Node handles can also be moved between maps or sets of the same type, with no copy of the value. Inserting fails (and returns the node) if the new key already exists.

code.title: Strict weak ordering and equivalence

followUps:
Write the comparator so that it first compares priority in reverse, then compares name normally, and returns false when both are equal.

auto cmp = [](const T& a, const T& b) {
  if (a.priority != b.priority)
    return a.priority > b.priority;  // higher first
  return a.name < b.name;             // then A to Z
};

Check: {3,"b"} comes before {1,"a"}, and {3,"a"} before {3,"b"}. Equal elements return false both ways, so it is a strict weak ordering. Alternative: std::tie(b.priority, a.name) < std::tie(a.priority, b.name).

The state used for comparison must not change while the element is inside a set because the tree placed the element by that state, so changing it silently puts the element in the wrong position and breaks lookups.

Example: a set ordered by age holds 20, 30, 40. If the 30 becomes 10 in place, the tree still thinks it sits between 20 and 40, so find(10) searches left and misses it, and a later insert may create duplicates. That is why set elements are const. To change a key, extract the node, change it, and re-insert, or erase and insert again.

code.title: Hash flooding with identity hash vs splitmix64

followUps:
reserve() does not save you because it only sets the number of buckets; the attacker's keys are chosen to land in the same bucket for that bucket count, so one chain still gets all of them.

It prevents rehashing, not collisions. If keys are multiples of the bucket count, with the identity hash every key maps to bucket 0 regardless of how many buckets exist. With 200,000 such keys, each insert walks a growing chain, about 2 x 1010 steps in total. Fix the hash itself (mix the bits and add a random seed), not the size.

splitmix64 is a short function that mixes all bits of a 64-bit number so that nearby inputs give unrelated outputs.

uint64_t mix(uint64_t x) {
  x += 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL;
  x = (x ^ (x >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
  x = (x ^ (x >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
  return x ^ (x >> 31);
}

Use it as mix(x + SEED) where SEED comes from chrono::steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch().count(), so the attacker cannot predict the layout.

code.title: Tiny flat_map versus map and unordered_map

followUps:
absl::btree_map beats std::map when you have many entries and mostly lookups and ordered scans, because each node holds many keys in contiguous memory, so there are far fewer cache misses.

For a million int keys std::map needs about 20 pointer hops, btree needs about 4 node visits, and it uses roughly half the memory (no 3 pointers and a colour per key). Typical speed-ups are 2 to 3 times for lookup and more for iteration. It loses when you need stable addresses of elements (inserts shift keys inside a node) or when the map is tiny.

std::map costs about 40 to 50 bytes per element on top of the data, unordered_map about 30 to 40, and flat_map almost none.

For a map of 4-byte int to 4-byte int with 1,000,000 entries: std::map node = 3 pointers (24 bytes) + colour (8 with padding) + 8 data + malloc header (about 16) = about 48 MB. unordered_map: a node of 8 data + next pointer + cached hash (about 24, rounded by malloc to 32), plus an 8-byte bucket pointer, about 40 MB. flat_map: two vectors of 4 MB each, 8 MB total.

code.title: RandomizedSet with O(1) getRandom

followUps:
To allow duplicates keep, for each value, the set of positions where it occurs: unordered_map<T, unordered_set<size_t>>, and the vector holds repeated values.

insert: push_back and add the index to the set. erase(x): take any index i from x's set, swap the last element into i (fix the moved value's set: remove its old last index, add i), pop_back. getRandom stays a random index, so a value with 3 copies is 3 times as likely, which is the usual expectation. Everything is O(1) on average.

To make getRandom weighted, keep a prefix-sum array of the weights and pick a random number in [0, total), then binary search for it, so each value is chosen in proportion to its weight.

Example: weights 1, 3, 6 give prefix sums 1, 4, 10. A random number from 0 to 9 maps to: 0 gives item A, 1 to 3 give item B, 4 to 9 give item C (probabilities 10%, 30%, 60%). Query is O(log n) with upper_bound. Updates cost O(n) with plain prefix sums, so with frequent changes use a Fenwick tree (O(log n) for both).
